place.zh: 沂中医 · 体育场 · 九月

setup.zh: 入学第十二天，体测一千米。沈芒当着半个看台的女生，跑死在第四百米上，吐在一个女孩递来的塑料袋里。
setup.en: Twelfth day of term, the 1000-metre fitness test. In front of half a stand of girls, Shen Mang died at the four-hundred-metre mark and threw up into a plastic bag a girl held out.

recap.zh: 一千米四分五十八，没及格，吐了；第二天他在篮球队的报名表上签了字。
recap.en: The thousand metres in 4′58″, a fail, and he threw up; the next day he signed the basketball team's form.

zh: 一只白球鞋，一个小本子。
en: A white sneaker, a small notebook.

story.zh:
入学第十二天，沈芒当着半个看台的女生，跑死在了一千米的第四百米上。

说「死」，未免夸张；可在他自己看来，一个字也不夸张。嗓子眼里像塞了一把烧红的铁砂，两条腿是别人借给他、这会儿正急着要回去的。他张大了嘴喘，又快又浅，一口刚吸到喉咙，下一口已经急着出来，两口气在嗓子眼里撞个满怀，谁也不肯让谁。

一分钟以前，他还跑在第二。哨子一响他就冲了出去——他怕的倒不是一千米，是看台，女生组正坐在那儿等着跑八百。

此人姓沈，名芒，十八岁，沂州中医药大学针灸推拿学专业大一新生；学校在山东临沂城北，沂河西岸。若问他有什么特长：话多。这会儿，一个字也说不出来了。

终点线上，体育部的雷老师按停秒表，像念一张罚单：「沈芒，四分五十八。及格线四分三十二。九月二十四号补测。」

沈芒膝盖一软便要往地上蹲，雷老师一把薅住他的后领子：「别蹲！走！」走了没几步，胃里翻江倒海。一只手往他手里塞了个塑料袋：「吐这里。跑道明天还要用。」

是个女孩的声音，不高，不急。他弯下腰，把中午那碗牛肉面原原本本还给了这个世界。眼前一阵一阵发黑，黑里头恍恍惚惚坐着他太奶，在老家院子的小板凳上冲他招手：「芒啊，来，饺子刚出锅。」他太奶走了六年了。

等那阵黑过去，他只看见一双白球鞋、一截蓝色的志愿者马甲、一只攥着小本子的手。那声音在头顶上说：「今年头一个。」笔尖在本子上沙沙记了一笔。

他最怕的，就是这一笔。他提着一袋自己的午饭，腿软得只想坐，到底没坐，一步一步把那一圈走完了。

那天夜里，六一七宿舍。报到那天他把三栋楼各爬了一遍六层才找着这间屋，屋里从此管他叫「沈忙」。眼镜扶了扶眼镜：「沈忙，学生手册上写着，体测不到五十分，只发结业证，没有毕业证。」

上铺的老蔡探出头：「你作文写得那么好，怎么跑来学中医了？」沈芒道：「调剂的。第六个志愿是我妈填的。」他说这话时，眼睛看着墙上那幅二十四节气的挂图，没看人。

眼镜从桌上拿起一本图书馆的旧书，《抱朴子内篇》，一字一顿地念：「夫人在气中，气在人中。」念完抬眼看他，「你吐进袋子的是面条。气吐不进去——真吐干净了，那叫断气。」

十点，他妈打来视频。不知哪位家长热心，把看台上拍的那段转进了新生家长群。「你爸看了八遍。」他爸的脸挤进镜头，郑重其事：「芒啊，跑不过，就走。走，不丢人。我当年体测，就是走完的。」他妈道：「倒数第二。」他爸道：「倒数第一那个，是抬下去的。」

半夜他饿醒了，借着路灯，指头在挂图上找到芒种——他是芒种那天生的——往前挪一格：小满。底下一行小字：「麦粒渐饱，尚未全满。」

「小满，」他小声念，「还没满。听着像个永远吃不饱的。」

肚子咕噜一声，替小满答应了。

第二天中心广场百团大战，他是去棋社的——查过了，下棋全程坐着。半路被一面手写的横幅挡住：「校篮球队 · 招新」。折叠桌后头坐着一个马尾辫的女孩，面前摊着那个小本子。

这个声音他认得。从看见她的脸，到拿起报名表，一共三秒；有一秒半是在找笔。

她翻到一页，念道：「沈芒。前两百米三十九秒，全组第二；四百米，第十；最后一个过线。吐了。」抬眼，「头两百米是欠着氧气跑的。欠了要还，所以停下来还喘半天。」

原来那一笔记的是这个。他的耳朵烧了起来。

一堵墙晃了过来，一米九几，手腕上一块表，手里一只大摇杯，歪头看他的报名表：「沈芒。芒硝的芒？泻药。」伸出一只锅盖似的手，「马小宝。中药学大三。家里开药房的。小意思。」

她递给沈芒一个球：「投一个。」球飞得很高，很有信心，越过篮筐，越过篮板，不偏不倚，砸翻了马小宝的摇杯，半杯蛋白粉淌在他的球鞋上。马小宝低头看了看，笑了：「没事。一双鞋。」擦得很慢，「家里还有。」

旁边一个大一的大高个刚签完名，看了一眼这阵势，搁下笔，转身往街舞社的摊子去了。她在本子上记：「刘一鸣，一米八八。跑了。」马小宝乐了：「大刘跑了，来了个小沈。」

「篮球队收人，看两样：能不能练，肯不肯来。」她不理他，「能不能练，我不知道；肯不肯来——你吐完了，没坐下，自己走完了那一圈。」她指了指最底下一栏，「本人签字。」

她叫阿禾。夜里，她发来一张表，「沈芒 · 补测前十四天」，末一条：「补测那天，前两百米不许快过四十五秒。你是死在前两百米上的。」底下另起一行：「鸡蛋一个一块二，十四天，十六块八，记在你名下。」

沈芒回：「过了有奖吗？」对面回：「看你补测成绩。」
story.en:
On his twelfth day at university, in front of half a grandstand of girls, Shen Mang died running the thousand metres, four hundred metres in.

"Died" may sound like an exaggeration; as far as he was concerned, it wasn't one word too strong. His throat felt stuffed with a fistful of red-hot iron grit, and his legs were on loan from someone who wanted them back right now. He gasped with his mouth wide open, fast and shallow: one breath had barely reached his throat before the next was rushing out, and the two collided in his windpipe, neither willing to give way.

A minute earlier he had been running second. He had shot off at the whistle — it wasn't the thousand metres he was afraid of, it was the grandstand, where the girls' group sat waiting to run their eight hundred.

The young man's surname was Shen, given name Mang; eighteen years old, a first-year in Acupuncture and Tuina at Yizhou University of Chinese Medicine, north of Linyi city in Shandong, on the west bank of the Yi River. Ask what his talent was: talking. At this moment he couldn't get out a single word.

At the finish line Coach Lei of the PE department stopped his stopwatch and read it out like a ticket: "Shen Mang, four fifty-eight. Pass line is four thirty-two. Retest on the twenty-fourth of September."

Shen Mang's knees gave and he started to squat, but Coach Lei grabbed him by the back of the collar: "Don't squat! Walk!" A few steps on, his stomach heaved. A hand pushed a plastic bag into his hand: "In here. The track's needed tomorrow."

A girl's voice, not loud, not hurried. He bent over and returned the bowl of beef noodles from lunch to the world exactly as he had received it. His sight went black in waves, and in the black, dimly, sat his great-grandma on a little stool in the yard back home, waving him over: "Mang, come on, the dumplings are just out of the pot." His great-grandma had been gone six years.

When the black passed, all he could see was a pair of white sneakers, a strip of blue volunteer vest, and a hand gripping a small notebook. The voice above his head said, "First one this year." A pen tip scratched a line in the notebook.

That line was exactly what he dreaded most. Holding a bag of his own lunch, legs so weak all he wanted was to sit, he didn't sit after all, and walked the rest of the lap step by step.

That night, dorm Room 617. On registration day he had climbed all six floors of three buildings before he found the room, and ever since the room had called him "Shen Busy." Specs pushed up his glasses: "Shen Busy, the student handbook says if you score under fifty on the fitness test, you only get a certificate of completion, no diploma."

Old Cai poked his head over from the top bunk: "You write such good essays — how'd you end up studying Chinese medicine?" Shen Mang said, "Reassigned. My sixth choice. My mom filled it in." As he said it he was looking at the chart of the twenty-four solar terms on the wall, not at anyone.

Specs picked up an old library book from the desk, the *Baopuzi, Inner Chapters*, and read it out word by word: "Man is within qi, and qi is within man." He looked up. "What you threw up into the bag was noodles. Qi doesn't go in a bag — if you really threw it all up, that's called breathing your last."

At ten his mom video-called. Some helpful parent had forwarded the clip filmed from the grandstand to the freshman parents' group. "Your dad's watched it eight times." His dad's face squeezed into the frame, very solemn: "Mang, if you can't run it, walk it. Walking's no shame. When I did my fitness test, I walked the whole thing." His mom said, "Second to last." His dad said, "The one who came last got carried off."

In the middle of the night hunger woke him. By the streetlight his finger found Grain in Ear on the chart — he was born on the day of Grain in Ear — and moved back one square: Lesser Fullness. Beneath it, a line of small print: "The wheat grains fill out, not yet full."

"Lesser Fullness," he read under his breath. "Not yet full. Sounds like somebody who never gets enough to eat."

His stomach rumbled, answering for Lesser Fullness.

The next day the central square held the big club fair. He was heading for the chess club — he'd checked: chess was sitting down the whole time. Halfway there a handwritten banner blocked his way: "University Basketball Team · Recruiting." Behind a folding table sat a girl with a ponytail, the little notebook open in front of her.

He knew that voice. From seeing her face to picking up the sign-up form took three seconds; a second and a half of it was spent looking for a pen.

She turned to a page and read: "Shen Mang. First two hundred metres in thirty-nine seconds, second in the group; at four hundred, tenth; last across the line. Threw up." She looked up. "You ran the first two hundred on borrowed oxygen. What you borrow you pay back, so you're still gasping long after you stop."

So that was what the line had recorded. His ears began to burn.

A wall swayed over, six foot three or four, a watch on its wrist, a big shaker bottle in its hand, and tilted its head to read his form: "Shen Mang. Mang as in mangxiao, Glauber's salt? That's a laxative." It held out a hand the size of a pot lid. "Ma Xiaobao. Third-year, Chinese Pharmacy. Family runs a pharmacy. Small stuff."

She handed Shen Mang a ball: "Shoot one." The ball flew high, full of confidence, over the rim, over the backboard, and landed square on Ma Xiaobao's shaker, knocking it over; half a bottle of protein shake ran across his sneakers. Ma Xiaobao looked down and laughed. "No problem. Just a pair of shoes." He wiped them very slowly. "Got more at home."

A tall first-year beside them had just signed his name; he took one look at the scene, put down the pen, turned, and walked off toward the street-dance club's stall. She wrote in her notebook: "Liu Yiming, 1.88 m. Ran." Ma Xiaobao was delighted: "Big Liu runs off, and in comes Little Shen."

"The basketball team looks at two things: can you train, and will you show up." She ignored him. "Whether you can train, I don't know. Whether you'll show up — you finished throwing up, didn't sit down, and walked the rest of that lap yourself." She pointed to the bottom box. "Your signature."

Her name was Ahe. That night she sent him a sheet, "Shen Mang · Fourteen Days to the Retest," and the last item read: "On retest day, the first two hundred metres no faster than forty-five seconds. You died in the first two hundred." Below, on a new line: "Eggs at 1.20 yuan each, fourteen days, 16.80 yuan, on your account."

Shen Mang replied: "Is there a prize if I pass?" The reply came: "Depends on your retest time."

exits.means: goes on to the first week of classes
